Leverage and drawdowns: why a 20% asset loss can halve the money you own

Follow own capital through a leveraged loss. Separate the asset move, unchanged loan principal and interest already paid, then compare household resources across four stress charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate an investment value, its loan and outside interest cash

Interactive planning lab

Sale proceeds remaining after the loan principal is repaid$10,000
Investment result after all outside interest payments-$17,200
Monthly interest paid from the household budget$200

Original mathematical illustration of a fixed interest-only loan invested with own capital at time zero. The asset-change input is one cumulative change over the entire selected horizon, not an annual rate. Asset value never falls below zero, but debt is not limited by remaining asset value. Interest is the nominal annual rate divided by twelve on unchanged loan principal, paid monthly from new outside household resources. It is not capitalized. At the common endpoint the investment is sold and the full original loan principal is repaid. The no-loan comparison starts with the same own capital and receives identical outside monthly resources, retaining them in zero-return cash rather than paying interest. No income distributions, taxes, deduction, fee, collateral rule, credit qualification, margin call, forced sale, loan repayment restriction or early cash need is modeled. Negative residuals are arithmetic funding gaps, not determinations of legal liability. No investment or borrowing strategy is recommended.

The central idea

A lender’s principal remains owed when an investment falls. Measure the remaining own capital and the interest cash already paid, rather than interpreting the asset’s percentage change as the household’s full result.

01

Write down the asset and the liability separately

Borrowing can make an investment account larger without adding the same amount to household net worth. A CAD 30,000 loan adds CAD 30,000 of purchasing power and a CAD 30,000 liability. The account statement shows the investment; a complete plan also needs the debt.

The Autorité des marchés financiers explains the risks of borrowing to invest, including that the loan and interest remain payable when investments lose value. The charts isolate that arithmetic with original inputs. They do not determine whether a lender will approve a loan or whether borrowing is appropriate for a particular household.

The example invests CAD 20,000 of own capital with CAD 30,000 of borrowed principal, creating a CAD 50,000 investment. Interest is paid from new outside household money. The investment is sold at the selected final date and the original loan principal is repaid then. There is no assumption that the investment pays distributions to cover the monthly bill.

02

A 20% asset loss can remove half the original own capital

The default asset-change input is a cumulative negative 20% over the entire three-year horizon. It is not negative 20% in each year. The CAD 50,000 investment therefore falls by CAD 10,000 and is sold for CAD 40,000.

Repaying the unchanged CAD 30,000 loan leaves CAD 10,000. Relative to the original CAD 20,000 of own capital, half remains before considering outside interest payments. The asset’s 20% decline and the own-capital reduction use different denominators.

The sale waterfall makes the distinction explicit: own money plus the borrowed principal, plus the investment-value change, less the loan repaid. If sale proceeds are below the loan, the arithmetic endpoint becomes negative. The chart retains that gap rather than flooring it at zero. It does not determine the borrower’s legal liability, the availability of other collateral or contractual guarantees.

03

Paying the interest elsewhere does not remove its cost

At the assumed nominal annual loan rate of 8%, the unchanged CAD 30,000 principal requires CAD 200 of interest each month. Across three years, the household supplies CAD 7,200 of outside cash. The model pays it as it arises, so it is not added to the loan balance.

The account’s sale residual is CAD 10,000, but the complete investment result also subtracts the CAD 20,000 initially supplied and the CAD 7,200 interest paid along the way. That leaves a negative CAD 17,200 result. It is an amount of money lost across the modeled cash flows, not an annualized return or a statement that the whole loss occurred at the final sale.

The annual-interest bars show alternative assumed loan rates on the same principal. These cash commitments exist even when the asset supplies no cash income. A principal repayment schedule, loan fees, changing interest rates or capitalized interest would require another ledger. None is silently included here.

04

Compare equal household resources, not a free interest budget

A no-loan alternative invests only the same CAD 20,000 of own capital. To keep the household-resource comparison consistent, it also receives the same CAD 200 of outside money each month. It retains that money in zero-return cash because it has no loan-interest bill to pay.

After the same cumulative 20% investment decline, the unborrowed investment is CAD 16,000. Adding CAD 7,200 of retained cash gives CAD 23,200 of ending resources. The borrowed alternative has CAD 10,000 after repaying principal. The difference is negative CAD 13,200.

That difference consists of the CAD 6,000 loss on the borrowed investment portion and CAD 7,200 of interest paid instead of retained. The extra monthly money is not treated as an investment gain in the no-loan case. Both households received it; one kept it and the other used it to service debt. This is why the ending-resource lines and the net-investment-result headline answer related but different questions.

05

A positive result does not establish that borrowing helped

Change the cumulative investment move to positive 20% while leaving the three-year horizon and 8% nominal loan rate unchanged. The CAD 50,000 investment becomes CAD 60,000, leaving CAD 30,000 after loan repayment. Subtracting own starting capital and outside interest produces a positive CAD 2,800 investment result.

The no-loan alternative has a CAD 24,000 investment plus CAD 7,200 of retained outside cash, or CAD 31,200. The borrowed choice is still CAD 1,200 behind on the same household-resource basis. Making money overall and benefiting from the borrowing are therefore separate tests.

In this simple zero-fee, zero-tax, zero-cash-return setup, the incremental borrowed portion needs a cumulative asset gain greater than the loan rate multiplied by the number of years to finish ahead. At the defaults that threshold is 24% over three years. It is not a guaranteed return, a quoted loan hurdle, or a sufficient assessment of risk. The asset path may also create cash or contractual problems before the endpoint.

06

Use the stress views to identify obligations outside the investment

The signed matrix changes cumulative asset moves and loan sizes. It deducts the original own capital and every outside interest payment from sale proceeds after repaying principal. More borrowing increases both market exposure and required interest cash. Negative cells remain visible; the matrix does not attach a probability to them.

Real borrowing can add collateral requirements, early demands for repayment, trading restrictions, fees and tax questions. The illustration intentionally calculates none of those. Its fixed principal, fixed interest rate and ability to wait until the endpoint are assumptions that would need to be supported by an actual agreement. In particular, these charts must not be used to estimate a margin call or a permitted brokerage borrowing limit.

Begin a household review with the money required for bills, reserves and debt service independently of investment performance. Then record the actual liability beside the asset and trace interest payments from their real cash source. The useful lesson is the reconciliation: asset value, loan principal, remaining own capital and cash already paid are different quantities, and a plan needs all of them.
